title: How to use a magnetic chart keeper for cross-stitch
subtitle: Tracking your row position with a magnetic board and line guide
excerpt: A magnetic chart keeper is a magnetised board that holds a printed chart flat while a magnetic ruler or strip marks the current working row. The ruler slides down the chart row by row as stitching progresses, masking the completed rows above and the unworked rows below. It removes the need to annotate the chart and keeps the working line easy to find.
sourceNotes: Magnetic chart keeper use for counted cross-stitch. Standard craft accessory guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: A magnetic chart keeper holds a printed or photocopied chart flat and provides a sliding magnetic strip that marks the current working row. The strip covers completed rows and rests below the row being worked so the eye is drawn directly to the active line. It is especially useful for designs with many repeating rows on the same
Setting up and using the keeper

Print the chart at a size where each symbol square is large enough to see clearly. A square smaller than 4 mm is difficult to mark or track with a magnetic ruler. Resize the print if the default chart print is very small.

Place the chart on the magnetic board. The board is magnetised and the chart is held in place by the magnetic strip rather than by clips or tape. Align the chart so the horizontal rows are parallel to the top and bottom of the board.
Position the magnetic ruler below the first working row. The ruler should cover the rows below and leave the current row fully visible above it. Check that the full width of the row is visible.

Stitch the current row, then move the magnetic ruler down by one chart row. The completed row is now above the ruler and the next row is revealed below. Continue moving the ruler down one row at a time as each row is completed.

When setting the project aside, note the current row number before putting the chart down. When returning, the ruler position should confirm which row you are on. Cross-check against the fabric before continuing to ensure the fabric and chart are aligned.

items.symptom: The chart slips out of position on the board
items.cause: The chart paper is too thick for the magnet to hold securely, or the board magnet has weakened.
items.fix: Add a small piece of magnetic tape to the back of the chart's top edge, then attach it to the board. This gives the board's magnet a metal surface to grip. Alternatively, use a small adhesive magnetic strip along the chart edges.

items.symptom: You lost your position and are not sure which row the ruler should be on
items.cause: The ruler was moved before verifying that the previous row was complete, or the row number was not noted when the project was set aside.
items.fix: Compare the stitching on the fabric against the chart row by row from the top down, or from the last row you are certain of. Move the ruler to match the verified position. Going back to a known correct row and counting forward is more reliable than trying to estimate from where the stitching ends.

content.text: Magnetic chart keepers work best for designs stitched row by row across the full width. For designs stitched one colour area at a time rather than row by row, pencil marking of the chart is often more practical, as the magnetic ruler is most useful when a single line tracks your position from start to finish.
